help.title: Help
help.lead: How Showtime works, what its numbers mean and where its limits are.
help.how_lead: Three steps, from your venue to a plan you can hand to your team.
help.step1_body: Pick it on the map, describe it in one sentence, or start from a sample. Then check the doors and how many people are coming.
help.step2_body: The AI tries what could go wrong, like a blocked gate or a sudden rush. Each idea is simulated, and a fix is kept only if it measurably helps.
help.step3_body: See if the plan holds, what the AI changed and when to start evacuating. Download the report for your team.
help.numbers_lead: Every number comes from a formula, the simulator or a published source. The AI never makes one up.
help.n_evac_body: How long until 95 out of 100 people are out, counted from when they start moving. Shorter is better.
help.n_density_body: How tightly people stand. Around 2 is a packed crowd that still moves. From 3.5 people can't move freely (warning); from 5, crush risk rises (danger).
help.n_latest: Latest safe time to start evacuating
help.n_latest_body: The last moment to start an evacuation so that everyone is out, with a safety margin, before a hazard such as a strong gust arrives.
help.n_capacity_body: The most people your exits and floor space can handle, from published planning ratios.
help.levels_lead: Each number says where it comes from. The fuller the bar, the more certain the number.
help.level_instant_body: A formula from exit widths and walking distances. Ready in a moment. Good for comparing ideas.
help.level_quick_body: Every person is simulated for the first 3 minutes. Used to rank many ideas fast.
help.level_full_body: Every person is simulated until everyone is out. Shown as “Confirmed by simulation”.
help.limit_signoff: Licensed engineers and the authorities sign off on real plans.
help.limit_pushing: The simulation models walking and queueing, not pushing. High density is the warning sign for crush risk.
help.limit_stairs: Stairs are modelled as a queue with a fixed flow, not as a slope people walk on.
help.limit_weather: Weather forecasts smooth out sudden storm gusts. Enter your own gust when storms are possible.
help.limit_samples: Sample venues are examples. Check sizes against your real drawings.
help.glossary_lead: Words you will see in your plan, in plain language.
help.g_people_per_m2_body: How many people stand on one square metre. The main sign of crowd danger.
help.g_evac_body: Time until 95% of people are out, from when they start moving.
help.g_peak_body: The highest people per m² anywhere in the venue during the simulation.
help.g_latest: Latest safe time to start evacuating
help.g_latest_body: The last moment to start leaving so that everyone is out, with a margin, before the hazard.
help.g_capacity_body: The most people the exits and space can handle.
help.g_stress_test_body: A full simulation of your plan in which everyone leaves normally.
help.g_red_team_body: AI that plays the attacker: it tries realistic things that could go wrong, based on real crowd incidents.
help.g_fix_body: A change the AI proposes, like a wider gate or stewards guiding people. It is kept only if the simulation shows it helps.
help.g_blocked_exit_body: An exit that can't be used, for example because a gate is jammed or the route is unsafe.
help.g_hotspot_body: A place where the crowd got denser than the warning level.
help.g_counterflow_body: People moving against the crowd, for example walking in while others leave. A common factor in crushes.
help.g_reaction_body: Time between the alarm and people starting to move. Experts call it pre-movement time.
help.g_margin_body: Extra time added to the evacuation time to allow for surprises. Experts call it the safety factor.
help.g_planning_aid_body: Showtime helps you plan and decide. It is not a safety certification.
help.tech_lead: How the numbers are computed, for engineers and permit officers.
help.tech_instant_body: Walking distances on a grid that respects walls, a min-cost flow that assigns people to exits within each exit's capacity (1.3 people per metre of width per second, SFPE), and a queue at every exit. Takes a few milliseconds. Used for 'Break it yourself' and to rank attacks.
help.tech_sim_body: Every person is simulated with JuPedSim's collision-free speed model (Δt 0.025–0.05 s) inside an isolated Docker sandbox with no network. Body radius 0.22 m, walking speed 1.34 ± 0.26 m/s (5% slow walkers). Upper floors are simulated first; stairs pass at most 1 person per metre per second.
help.tech_density_body: People counted on a 1 m grid, smoothed over about 2–3 m² and divided by the walkable area of each cell. Warning at 3.5, danger at 5 people per m² (sustained for at least 5 s).
help.tech_evac_body: Seconds until 95% of people have passed an exit, from the moment they start moving. Pre-movement time is added separately in the countdown.
help.tech_wind_body: Pynite frame model of the stage roof with ASCE 7 wind pressure q = 0.613·Kz·Kzt·Kd·V². Gust speed at which ballast stops resisting uplift, sliding or overturning. A screening estimate, not a structural design.
help.tech_latest: Latest safe time to start evacuating
help.tech_latest_body: T_hazard − (pre-movement + evacuation time × safety factor). The hazard is the first forecast gust above the wind limit (Open-Meteo) or the scenario time when a route is lost.
help.verdict_lead: Your plan says two things: what the numbers show, and how sure they are.
help.v_holds_body: No tested scenario pushed the crowd past the danger density, and everyone got out.
help.v_at_risk_body: The crowd got close to the danger density, or above the warning level for a while.
help.v_fails_body: In at least one scenario the crowd reached the danger density or people could not get out.
help.v_confirmed_body: The plan was simulated in full, before and after the changes, until everyone was out.
help.v_partly_body: Full simulations ran but stopped at their time limit; the last part of the evacuation is estimated.
help.v_unconfirmed_body: The verdict rests on quick simulations, the instant estimate or a preview. Run the test again with the simulator on, or keep the changes and test again, to confirm it.
help.v_failed_body: The full simulations did not finish (time limit or an error); the numbers shown are estimates.

home.title: Plan a safe event in minutes
home.lead: Will everyone get out safely? Show us where your event is: AI agents write what could go wrong, a real crowd simulator tests it in sealed sandboxes, and you get a tested plan you can hand to your team.
home.way_map_lead: Search your place and click the building, park or field.
home.way_describe_lead: Write one sentence about the place. The AI draws it for you.
home.way_sample_lead: No venue yet? Start with a ready-made hall, field or street.
home.trust: Planning aid, not a safety certification. Every number comes from a simulation or a formula.
home.describe_lead: The AI drafts a venue from your words. You check and correct it next.
home.describe_ph: A 40 by 25 m hall with a stage on the north wall, two doors on the south side, 1,200 people
home.example_hall: A 40 by 25 m conference hall with a stage on the north wall, two 2 m doors on the south wall, 900 people
home.example_field: An open field 80 by 50 m with a stage in the north, two gates in the south and 5,000 people
home.example_alley: A narrow street 4 m wide and 50 m long with exits at both ends and 1,500 people
home.design_failed: The AI couldn't draft this venue.
home.try_template: Start from a template instead, then adjust it.
home.no_plans_body: Pick your place on the map above to start your first plan.
home.more_ways: Need a real place on the map or a file import?

why.confirmed: Full simulations of the plan, before and after the changes, ran until everyone was out.
why.partially_confirmed: The full simulations reached their time limit before everyone was out, so the end of the evacuation is estimated.
why.failed: The full simulations meant to check this plan did not finish, so the numbers come from estimates.
why.preview: The simulator was not running, so these numbers are a preview, not a simulation.
why.estimate: The final check used the instant estimate (a formula), not a full simulation.
why.quick: Only quick simulations of the first minutes checked it; no full simulation ran to the end.
why.unfinished: The final simulation did not finish, so nothing confirms the result.
why.no_final: No full simulation of the final plan with its changes has run, so nothing confirms the result yet.
why.legacy: This test was made before Showtime recorded how its results were confirmed, so it counts as not confirmed. Test again to know.

analyst.unchecked: The written summary was left out: it quoted numbers the code did not compute.

analyst.no_output: The code returned nothing to show.

analyst.ai_down: The AI isn't answering, so I can't write an analysis right now. What-ifs still work.

userscripts.title: Scripts
userscripts.lead: Bring your own model: write or upload a script and run it in a sealed sandbox (no network, time and memory limits). Analysis scripts read a simulated run; scenario scripts change the crowd while it runs.
userscripts.empty_body: Start a new analysis script, or upload a .py file.

userscripts.kind_analysis_help: Reads a simulated run with showtime_data (trajectories, density, exits, zones). End by setting output = {...}.
userscripts.kind_scenario_help: Runs during a quick simulation: on_step(view, act) is called every few seconds and may close or open exits, redirect people, add people or slow the crowd.

rewind.body: Go back to the second the worst attack was most dangerous and try responses from that same second. Each response runs in its own sandbox, all at once, and is compared with doing nothing.

rewind.lower_better: Lower is better in every column. The small number under each value is the change against doing nothing.

range.title: How sure are these numbers?
range.body: Headcount and walking speed are estimates. This runs the result your plan rests on again with 20% fewer and 20% more people, and with everyone walking 15% slower and 15% faster: same crowd seed, layout and scenario.
range.holds_all: The plan holds under every assumption tested.
range.incomplete: Not every run finished, so the range is incomplete.
range.over: Range over {n} runs that finished, the plan as tested included.

stress.title: Stress test at scale
stress.body: Run every attack against your plan and against each kept change, several times with different random crowds, all in parallel sandboxes.
stress.interrupted: The stress test was cut off. Start it again.

validation.title: How good is the simulator?
validation.lead: We gave the simulator a published experiment with real people walking through a bottleneck, and compared how many people per second got through.
validation.what: The experiment: {n} runs of the Jülich bottleneck series (Düsseldorf, 2006), about 175 people each, bottleneck widths {min}–{max} m. We built the same layout and headcount, simulated each width {seeds} times with the app's default settings, and measured the flow at the bottleneck entrance with the same method for both.
validation.verdict_lower: At every width the simulator let fewer people through than the real crowd did: its flow is {median}% lower (median over {n} widths).
validation.verdict_higher: The simulator let more people through than the real crowd did: its flow is {median}% higher (median over {n} widths).
validation.verdict_close: The simulator's flow is within {median}% of the real crowd's (median over {n} widths).
validation.meaning_title: What this means for your plan
validation.meaning_close: Through doors and narrow passages the simulated crowd gets through at about the same rate as these real people did, so evacuation times that are set by a bottleneck are realistic for a calm crowd like this one. Real crowds differ from these test participants: treat the times as a planning estimate, not as a safety margin.
validation.meaning_lower: Through doors and narrow passages the simulated crowd is slower than these real people were, so evacuation times that are set by a bottleneck come out longer than in the experiment. That errs on the cautious side, but treat it as a known limit, not as a safety margin: real crowds differ from these test participants.
validation.meaning_higher: Through doors and narrow passages the simulated crowd is faster than these real people were, so evacuation times that are set by a bottleneck may be too short. Add a margin.
validation.limits_title: What this check does not cover
validation.limit_forces: No pushing forces: simulated people steer around each other and never push; real crowds press and compress, especially under stress.
validation.limit_motivation: Motivation is not modelled: the participants were asked to walk normally. Hurried or competitive crowds flow differently.
validation.limit_density: Density cap: simulated bodies cannot overlap, so the model cannot reach the very high densities of a crush.
validation.limit_scope: One experiment, one group (young soldiers, 2006) and one kind of layout: a straight bottleneck 4 m long.
validation.legend_sim: Simulator (middle of {seeds} runs; band = lowest to highest)
validation.chart_label: Flow through a bottleneck against its width: real people compared with the simulator; median difference {median}%.
validation.table_caption: Measured and simulated flow per bottleneck width
validation.source: Data: {dataset}, DOI {doi}, licence {licence}. Method, assumptions and how to rerun: docs/VALIDATION.md.
